Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BEIJING, China (CNN) -- Consumers in Beijing's malls and shops are shunning the milk and poultry sections -- for good reasons. Poultry products, including eggs, may be contaminated with melamine through animal food. They are shocked and scared by the news headlines: some food produced in China is tainted with melamine. "Of course I'm worried," says a woman shopping in Nanxiaojie Market. Stop eating eggs? "That's not possible," she tells CNN. "If there's a problem with eggs, it should be solved fundamentally." Chinese premier Wen Jiabao says China will take steps to win back consumers. "We will use our actions and high quality of our food products to win the trust and confidence of Chinese people and people around the world," he told reporters at the end of a two-day summit of Asian and European leaders in Beijing last weekend.  Watch more about the tainted food scandal » . "Three minister-level officials have resigned and a government investigation is going on. Whoever is responsible must be brought to justice. We need to protect the Made in China brand," said Chinese analyst Victor Gao. But the problem could be more pervasive. The state-run Nanfang Daily published an investigative story saying that adding melamine into animal feed has become an "open secret." The report said adding melamine into feed started in the aquatic farming industry five years ago, as a way of faking higher protein levels.  Learn more about chemical melamine » . It then spread into other agro-industries such as poultry. Even more shocking is the allegation that the melamine added is from industrial waste material. CNN contacted the Ministry of Agriculture about the story, but got no immediate response. Two years ago, reports revealed pet food exported from China to the United States was spiked with melamine and had sickened and killed dogs. Several weeks ago, the food scandal spread to milk, biscuits and candies. Now, it is tainted eggs. So far, no illnesses or deaths have been linked to eggs. Tests in Hong Kong last week showed eggs exported by a Chinese company are contaminated with excessive levels of melamine. In recent days three other brands of eggs have also been found to contain the chemical. Small wonder egg sales at the Xinfadi, a wholesale market in Beijing, dropped by 10 percent this week, according to the state-run China Daily. Chinese officials say the source of the problem is melamine, an industrial chemical used to produce plastics and fertilizer. Melamine is high in nitrogen. Unscrupulous milk suppliers would water down milk and spike it with melamine -- but in amounts that allowed it to still pass quality tests. Agriculture experts speculate that eggs tainted with melamine may be the result of tainted feed given to hens. That begs the question: if melamine was in the animal feed, will it make into the meat, and into consumers' bodies? Ingesting melamine in large doses over an extended period of time could cause kidney stones and other illnesses, agriculture and health experts say. But taking in a small amount of melamine poses no such danger. "If it's taken over a long period of time, maybe, but if it's ingested only for short period of time it does not pose harm on animals," says He Jiguo, a professor of food science and nutrition at the China Agriculture University. He says the animals that end up being slaughtered do not live that long and do not actually ingest enough melamine for it to build up in their systems. The dogs and cats that were sickened in the United States were probably eating treats and meals tainted with melamine over a long period of time, he explains. Until the situation is resolved, worried grocery shoppers in Beijing say they'll just have to eat fewer eggs and more bean-products, like soybeans.

outputs.L1:
**BEIJING, China (CNN) —** Consumers in Beijing’s malls and shops are avoiding the milk and poultry sections—and with good reason. Poultry products, including eggs, may have been contaminated with melamine through animal feed.

Shoppers have been shocked and alarmed by headlines reporting that some food produced in China is tainted with melamine.

“Of course I’m worried,” said a woman shopping at Nanxiaojie Market. But stop eating eggs? “That’s not possible,” she told CNN. “If there’s a problem with eggs, it should be solved fundamentally.”

Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao said China would take steps to regain consumers’ trust.

“We will use our actions and the high quality of our food products to win the trust and confidence of Chinese people and people around the world,” he told reporters at the conclusion of a two-day summit of Asian and European leaders in Beijing last weekend.

*Watch more about the tainted food scandal »*

“Three minister-level officials have resigned, and a government investigation is underway. Whoever is responsible must be brought to justice. We need to protect the ‘Made in China’ brand,” said Chinese analyst Victor Gao.

But the problem could be more widespread. The state-run *Nanfang Daily* published an investigative report stating that adding melamine to animal feed has become an “open secret.” According to the report, the practice began in the aquaculture industry five years ago as a means of falsifying higher protein levels.

*Learn more about the chemical melamine »*

The practice subsequently spread to other agricultural industries, including poultry production. Even more alarming is the allegation that the melamine being added comes from industrial waste. CNN contacted the Ministry of Agriculture about the report but received no immediate response.

Two years ago, reports revealed that pet food exported from China to the United States had been spiked with melamine, sickening and killing dogs. Several weeks ago, the food scandal expanded to include milk, biscuits and candies. Now, tainted eggs have been identified.

So far, no illnesses or deaths have been linked to the eggs. However, tests conducted in Hong Kong last week showed that eggs exported by a Chinese company contained excessive levels of melamine. In recent days, three other egg brands have also been found to contain the chemical.

It is therefore little surprise that egg sales at Xinfadi, a wholesale market in Beijing, fell by 10 percent this week, according to the state-run *China Daily*.

Chinese officials say the source of the problem is melamine, an industrial chemical used to manufacture plastics and fertilizer. Melamine has a high nitrogen content. Unscrupulous milk suppliers would dilute milk with water and add melamine in quantities that still allowed the product to pass quality tests.

Agricultural experts speculate that melamine-tainted eggs may have resulted from contaminated feed given to hens. This raises another question: If melamine was present in animal feed, could it enter the meat and, ultimately, consumers’ bodies?

Agricultural and health experts say that ingesting large doses of melamine over an extended period could cause kidney stones and other illnesses. Consuming a small amount, however, poses no such danger.

“If it’s taken over a long period of time, maybe, but if it’s ingested only for a short period of time, it does not harm animals,” said He Jiguo, a professor of food science and nutrition at China Agricultural University.

He said animals raised for slaughter do not live long enough or ingest sufficient quantities of melamine for it to accumulate in their systems. The dogs and cats sickened in the United States were probably eating melamine-tainted treats and meals over an extended period, he explained.

Until the situation is resolved, worried grocery shoppers in Beijing say they will simply have to eat fewer eggs and more bean products, such as soybeans.

BEIJING, China (CNN) — Shoppers in Beijing are increasingly avoiding dairy and poultry aisles, and their concern is understandable. Reports indicate that eggs and other poultry products may have been exposed to melamine through contaminated animal feed.

News that some Chinese-made foods contain the chemical has left consumers alarmed. A shopper at Nanxiaojie Market told CNN she was “of course” concerned. Asked whether she would stop eating eggs, she said that was unrealistic and argued that any safety issue involving eggs needed to be addressed at its source.

Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao has promised measures to restore public confidence. Speaking to journalists after a two-day summit of Asian and European leaders in Beijing last weekend, he said China would regain the trust of people both at home and abroad through concrete action and the high quality of its food products.

Chinese analyst Victor Gao said three officials holding ministerial rank had stepped down and that a government inquiry was underway. He added that everyone responsible should face justice and stressed the importance of safeguarding the “Made in China” label.

Evidence suggests, however, that the contamination may be more widespread. An investigation published by the state-controlled Nanfang Daily described the practice of mixing melamine into livestock feed as an “open secret.” According to the newspaper, the practice began five years earlier in aquaculture, where melamine was used to create the false appearance of higher protein content. It later expanded into other agricultural sectors, including poultry production. More disturbing still, the report alleged that the melamine came from industrial waste.

CNN requested comment from China’s Ministry of Agriculture but did not receive an immediate reply.

Melamine contamination had surfaced before. Two years earlier, reports showed that pet food shipped from China to the United States had been adulterated with the chemical, causing illness and death among dogs. Several weeks before the latest developments, the food-safety crisis had widened to include milk, cookies and candy. Eggs have now joined that list, although no sicknesses or deaths have so far been connected to contaminated eggs.

Tests conducted in Hong Kong last week found excessive melamine in eggs exported by one Chinese company. Three additional egg brands were subsequently discovered to contain the chemical. Against that background, egg sales at Xinfadi, a Beijing wholesale market, fell 10 percent during the week, according to the state-run China Daily.

Chinese authorities identify melamine as the substance at the center of the problem. It is an industrial chemical used in manufacturing plastics and fertilizer and contains a high level of nitrogen. Dishonest milk suppliers had diluted milk with water and then added enough melamine to make the product appear acceptable in quality tests.

Agricultural specialists believe contaminated feed given to hens could explain how melamine entered eggs. That possibility raises another concern: whether the chemical could also pass into animal meat and eventually into people who eat it.

Agriculture and health experts say consuming large quantities of melamine over a prolonged period can lead to kidney stones and other medical problems. Small amounts, however, are not considered to present the same risk.

He Jiguo, a food science and nutrition professor at China Agricultural University, said harm might occur after long-term exposure, but short-term consumption does not injure animals. He explained that animals raised for slaughter generally have short lives and therefore do not consume enough melamine for significant amounts to accumulate in their bodies. In his view, the cats and dogs that became ill in the United States were probably exposed over an extended period through contaminated meals and treats.

While authorities work to settle the issue, anxious Beijing shoppers say they will reduce their egg consumption and rely more heavily on bean-based foods such as soybeans.

Three minister-level officials have resigned, while authorities continue to investigate the individuals and companies responsible for the contamination.

outputs.L4:
Chinese consumers are increasingly avoiding milk, poultry, and eggs as concern grows that melamine-contaminated animal feed may have spread the chemical into a broad range of foods. The widening scandal has prompted official investigations, corporate apologies, resignations, and government promises to strengthen food-safety controls and restore public confidence.

Melamine, an industrial chemical used in products such as plastics and adhesives, can make food or feed appear to contain more protein than it actually does because common tests measure nitrogen rather than protein directly. Investigators suspect that some feed producers deliberately added melamine or melamine-containing “protein powder,” reportedly made in part from industrial waste, to low-quality ingredients in order to increase their apparent nutritional value and sell them at a higher price.

The latest fears emerged after tests detected melamine in eggs from several producers. Authorities began tracing the contamination back through the supply chain, focusing on feed supplied to poultry farms. Although no illnesses or deaths have been linked to the contaminated eggs, the findings have alarmed shoppers already shaken by the discovery of melamine in milk and infant formula.

Many consumers have responded by reducing or stopping purchases of dairy products, chicken, and eggs, while retailers and restaurants have faced pressure to identify the origin of their supplies. Parents in particular remain wary of official assurances, given the seriousness of the earlier dairy contamination and delays in disclosing the full extent of the problem.

The possibility that tainted feed was distributed widely has raised concerns that melamine could affect more than one branch of agriculture. If the same additives were used in feed for chickens, livestock, or farmed fish, contamination might not be limited to eggs or milk. Officials have therefore expanded inspections of farms, feed manufacturers, food-processing companies, and distribution networks.

The scandal has also exposed weaknesses in China’s rapidly expanding food-production system. Small farms often depend on outside suppliers for inexpensive feed, while long and complicated supply chains can make it difficult to determine where adulteration occurred. Local officials may also face economic pressure to protect major employers, creating doubts about whether problems are always reported quickly and transparently.

In response, the government has announced tighter testing, stronger supervision of feed producers, and harsher penalties for companies that deliberately adulterate food or agricultural products. Senior officials have pledged to close regulatory loopholes and punish both business operators and public employees found responsible. Several executives and officials have resigned or been removed as investigations continue.

The crisis is no longer viewed simply as an isolated case of misconduct by a few dairy companies. Evidence of contamination in other products suggests a broader pattern involving agricultural inputs and weak oversight. That possibility has deepened public suspicion and made it harder for the authorities to reassure consumers that the food supply is safe.

Internationally, the scandal threatens China’s efforts to present itself as a reliable producer of food and manufactured goods. Importing countries may impose additional tests, restrictions, or bans, increasing costs for legitimate exporters as well as for companies connected to the contamination. Even businesses that followed safety rules could suffer from declining trust in products carrying the “Made in China” label.

For now, officials emphasize that no illnesses or deaths have been attributed to melamine-tainted eggs. Nevertheless, the absence of reported casualties has done little to ease concern. The discovery has reinforced fears that contamination may be more widespread than previously acknowledged and that harmful substances can move from feed into animals and ultimately into food consumed by people.

Restoring confidence will require more than removing a few products from store shelves. Consumers and overseas buyers are likely to demand transparent investigations, regular publication of test results, stronger enforcement, and clear accountability throughout the supply chain. Until those measures produce visible results, the damage to public trust—and to the reputation of Chinese food exports—is likely to persist.

**Beijing consumers shun milk, eggs and poultry as melamine fears spread**

**BEIJING, China** — Beijing shoppers are cutting back on milk, eggs and poultry as China’s melamine contamination scandal widens beyond dairy products, raising fresh concerns about the country’s food-safety system.

Supermarkets in the Chinese capital have pulled or tested products after authorities detected melamine in some eggs and poultry feed. The industrial chemical had already been found in infant formula and other dairy products, sickening tens of thousands of children and contributing to several deaths.

Melamine, commonly used in plastics and fertilizers, can make products appear to contain more protein during routine testing. In high concentrations, it can cause kidney stones and kidney failure.

Chinese officials have said the chemical entered eggs and poultry through contaminated animal feed, reviving fears that the problem extends across the food chain. Authorities have ordered inspections of feed producers and food suppliers, while stores have increased testing and removed suspect brands.

For many Beijing consumers, official assurances have not been enough. Some shoppers are turning to imported milk, buying products marketed as organic, or avoiding dairy, eggs and chicken altogether.

The scandal began with reports of babies developing kidney problems after drinking formula made with melamine-tainted milk. It later expanded to include liquid milk, candy and other dairy-based products, prompting recalls in China and abroad.

The crisis has damaged confidence in Chinese food products and placed pressure on the government to strengthen regulation, improve transparency and punish companies accused of concealing contamination.

Health experts say consumers should follow official recall notices and buy products from reputable retailers. But as testing continues, many families in Beijing are taking a simpler precaution: leaving milk, poultry and eggs off the shopping list.

# Contaminated Feed Seen as Likely Route for Melamine in Chinese Eggs

**BEIJING —** The discovery of melamine in Chinese eggs raised fears that the industrial chemical at the center of the country’s tainted-milk scandal had spread more widely through the food chain, with contaminated poultry feed emerging as the most likely source.

The alarm grew in late 2008 after Hong Kong authorities detected melamine in eggs produced by a company in Dalian, in northeastern China. One sample reportedly contained 4.7 milligrams of melamine per kilogram, above Hong Kong’s legal limit of 2.5 milligrams per kilogram for most foods. Other jurisdictions began testing eggs and egg-based products, while Chinese officials inspected farms and feed suppliers.

Investigators focused on feed because melamine can make low-quality ingredients appear richer in protein. Standard protein tests estimate protein content by measuring nitrogen. Melamine is rich in nitrogen, so adding it to animal feed can artificially raise the test result even though the chemical has no nutritional value.

Chickens consuming contaminated feed can absorb small amounts of melamine, which may then pass into their eggs. The same route could potentially contaminate meat and other animal products, although the amount transferred depends on the level and duration of exposure.

Chinese agricultural officials said feed adulteration was a key line of inquiry and ordered broader checks of poultry farms and feed manufacturers. Authorities also moved to restrict or prohibit the deliberate addition of melamine to animal feed and pledged penalties for producers that violated safety rules. Some companies recalled eggs or suspended sales while tests were conducted.

The findings unsettled shoppers already shaken by the infant-formula crisis, in which melamine-tainted milk sickened hundreds of thousands of children and was linked to several deaths. Consumers in Hong Kong and mainland China told reporters that they were scrutinizing labels, avoiding unfamiliar brands and, in some cases, temporarily buying fewer eggs.

“I don’t know what is safe anymore,” was a common sentiment expressed in market interviews at the time. Parents were particularly concerned because eggs are widely eaten by children and used in cakes, biscuits and other processed foods.

Food-safety specialists said the egg contamination appeared to reflect a broader weakness in oversight rather than a problem unique to poultry. Feed passes through a long supply chain involving raw-material traders, processors, distributors and farms, making adulteration difficult to trace when records and inspections are inadequate.

Analysts also pointed to economic incentives. As prices for genuine protein ingredients such as soybean meal rose, unscrupulous suppliers could cut costs by substituting cheaper material and adding melamine to defeat routine quality tests. The practice highlighted the limits of relying on indirect measures of protein rather than testing specifically for adulterants.

Toxicologists stressed that melamine is not considered highly toxic in a single small dose, but repeated exposure can be dangerous. When melamine is consumed with related chemicals, crystals may form in the kidneys, potentially causing stones, urinary blockage or kidney failure. Infants and young children are especially vulnerable because of their size and developing organs.

Experts said the immediate risk from eating an occasional contaminated egg was likely to be lower than the risk posed by heavily adulterated infant formula consumed several times a day. Nevertheless, they argued that melamine had no legitimate place in food or feed and that exposure from multiple products could add up.

The episode prompted calls for more frequent feed inspections, better tracing of ingredients, direct testing for melamine and stronger enforcement throughout the agricultural supply chain. For consumers, it also deepened a crisis of confidence: contamination that began with milk now appeared capable of reaching the breakfast table through the animals themselves.

### Melamine-tainted eggs trigger concern in China

In late October 2008, Hong Kong food-safety authorities found excessive melamine in fresh brown eggs imported from Dalian, in mainland China. The eggs, produced by the Dalian Hanwei Enterprise Group, contained about **4.7 milligrams of melamine per kilogram**, nearly twice Hong Kong’s legal limit of **2.5 mg/kg**.

The discovery widened the melamine crisis beyond contaminated milk products. Investigators suspected that melamine had entered the eggs through adulterated poultry feed, where it could be added to make the feed appear richer in protein during testing. Hong Kong withdrew the affected eggs and expanded checks on eggs, meat and animal feed imported from the mainland. Chinese authorities also ordered inspections of poultry farms and feed producers.

Although officials said the contamination levels posed little immediate danger from normal egg consumption, public confidence weakened. Beijing media reported that egg sales in the capital fell by **at least 10%**, with some markets and retailers experiencing steeper declines; prices also dropped by roughly 10% in places. Consumers became cautious despite assurances that most eggs on sale had passed safety tests.

The incident demonstrated how the 2008 melamine scandal had spread through the food chain and intensified demands for stricter regulation of animal feed and agricultural products.

counterfactuals.output:
# Melamine Trail Widens in China, From Pet Food and Infant Formula to Poultry Feed and Eggs

**BEIJING, Nov. 1, 2008** — China’s widening melamine scandal, first brought to international attention by the deaths of pets in North America last year, has spread through the human food chain, from infant formula and other dairy products to livestock feed and eggs.

The discoveries have exposed a common fraud behind several food-safety crises: suppliers adding nitrogen-rich melamine to diluted or low-protein ingredients so they appear richer in protein during routine testing. The industrial chemical does not provide nutritional value and can damage the kidneys, particularly when combined with related compounds such as cyanuric acid.

The latest alarm came after Hong Kong authorities detected melamine in eggs imported from mainland China. Investigators traced at least some of the contamination to feed given to poultry, raising questions about whether the chemical may also have entered chicken meat and other animal products.

The finding has expanded a scandal that erupted publicly in September, when Chinese authorities acknowledged that milk powder produced by the Sanlu Group and numerous other dairy companies had been contaminated. At least four infants have died, more than 50,000 children have received medical treatment and thousands have been hospitalized, many with kidney stones or other urinary problems.

## Warning Signs in Pet Food

The first major warning came in early 2007, when dogs and cats in the United States, Canada and other countries began suffering kidney failure after eating commercial pet food.

A vast recall eventually covered more than 150 brands. Investigators found melamine in wheat gluten and rice-protein concentrate imported from China and used in pet foods. Some samples also contained cyanuric acid and related chemicals.

Neither melamine nor cyanuric acid is ordinarily considered highly toxic after a single, small exposure. Together, however, they can form insoluble crystals in the kidneys. Those crystals may block the kidney’s microscopic filtering structures and urinary passages, causing inflammation, stones, loss of kidney function and, in severe cases, death.

U.S. investigators concluded that the adulteration was economically motivated. Conventional protein tests estimate protein content by measuring nitrogen. Because melamine is about two-thirds nitrogen by weight, adding it can make a low-quality ingredient appear to contain more protein than it does.

Chinese authorities prosecuted managers linked to the contaminated ingredients and announced restrictions on melamine in feed. But the latest discoveries suggest that the practice persisted in parts of the supply chain.

## Milk Diluted, Then “Repaired”

The same basic method appears to have been used in China’s dairy industry.

Farmers or middlemen sometimes watered down raw milk to increase its volume. Watering reduces the milk’s apparent protein concentration, making the fraud detectable. Investigators say melamine was then added to restore the nitrogen reading and allow the diluted milk to pass crude protein checks.

The crisis became public after reports that infants who had consumed Sanlu milk powder were developing kidney stones. Sanlu, partly owned by New Zealand’s Fonterra cooperative, recalled large quantities of formula after testing found melamine.

Government inspections subsequently detected the chemical in products from 22 dairy companies. Contamination was found not only in infant formula but also in liquid milk, yogurt, ice cream, candy, biscuits and products containing Chinese milk powder.

Countries around the world banned or restricted Chinese dairy imports and recalled foods made with Chinese milk ingredients. The European Union, which does not import Chinese milk and dairy products directly, ordered additional testing of composite foods. Asian and African governments removed Chinese-made products from stores, while major food manufacturers began reviewing their ingredient sources.

The scandal severely damaged confidence in Chinese regulators because complaints about sick babies had circulated for weeks before the nationwide recall. Chinese officials later dismissed or detained local officials and company executives, while promising an overhaul of milk collection and testing.

## From Feed to Eggs

The discovery of melamine in eggs has opened a new front.

Hong Kong food-safety officials said tests on eggs from a producer in Dalian, in northeastern Liaoning province, found melamine at about **4.7 milligrams per kilogram**, above Hong Kong’s newly adopted limit of 2.5 milligrams per kilogram for most foods. Additional contaminated eggs were later reported from other mainland suppliers.

Mainland agricultural officials said tainted poultry feed was the likely source. The producer, Dalian Hanwei Enterprise Group, said contaminated feed ingredients had been supplied to its chickens.

Feed manufacturers have sometimes added melamine directly to feed or to protein ingredients such as soybean meal, fish meal and corn gluten in order to inflate protein-test results. The chemical can pass through an animal and appear in urine, tissues or eggs, although the amount transferred depends on the dose, duration of exposure and the animal’s metabolism.

Authorities ordered inspections of egg producers and animal-feed factories and said they would punish the illegal use of melamine. China’s agriculture ministry reiterated that melamine was prohibited in animal feed and began checking feed operations in several provinces.

The egg findings have prompted concern that contaminated feed could affect a wider range of foods, including poultry, pork, fish and farmed seafood. In 2007, U.S. officials quarantined some hogs and poultry after animals were fed scraps of melamine-contaminated pet food. Risk assessments concluded that the danger to people who ate meat from those animals was very low because the chemical had been greatly diluted.

The new Chinese cases are different, however, because investigators do not yet know how widespread the feed adulteration may be or how much melamine animals consumed.

## Kidney Damage Is the Central Risk

Melamine is used legally in the manufacture of plastics, laminates, adhesives, flame retardants and kitchenware. It is not approved as a food or feed additive.

Health experts say risk depends on both the amount consumed and the duration of exposure. Adults exposed to small quantities may excrete much of the chemical in urine without obvious injury. Infants are more vulnerable because their kidneys are still developing, their diets may consist almost entirely of formula and they consume more food relative to body weight.

Symptoms of serious exposure can include:

- Pain or difficulty during urination  
- Blood in the urine  
- Reduced urine output  
- Abdominal or back pain  
- Irritability in infants  
- Kidney stones  
- Acute kidney failure  

The interaction between melamine and cyanuric acid is an additional concern. When present together, they can bind into crystals even at doses that might cause less damage if either chemical were consumed alone. This mechanism was strongly implicated in the pet deaths of 2007.

Scientists have less information about chronic, low-dose exposure in humans. Animal studies have associated prolonged high exposure with bladder stones and tumors, although regulators say those findings do not mean that every trace of melamine creates an immediate cancer risk.

Hong Kong has established limits of 1 milligram per kilogram for foods intended for infants and young children and 2.5 milligrams per kilogram for other foods. Other governments and international agencies are reviewing their standards as testing expands.

## A Test of China’s Food-Safety System

The progression from pet food to infant formula and now to eggs indicates that melamine adulteration was not confined to one company or commodity. Instead, it appears to have exploited weaknesses in a fragmented food system involving small farms, independent milk collectors, feed dealers, ingredient brokers and large processors.

Routine nitrogen-based tests also provided an incentive for fraud because they could not distinguish genuine protein from melamine. More sophisticated methods, including chromatography and mass spectrometry, can detect the chemical directly but are more expensive and are not always available at local collection points.

Chinese leaders have promised stricter inspections, new dairy regulations and stronger criminal penalties. Inspectors have been sent to feed mills and farms, and authorities say dairy products are now being checked before reaching the market.

But each new discovery has renewed public doubt.

For parents, the milk scandal raised fears about the most basic source of infant nutrition. For consumers now confronting contaminated eggs, the central question is whether melamine has moved even farther through China’s farms and food factories than authorities have yet disclosed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a Beijing-datelined CNN article about public anxiety over tainted food, quoting Premier Wen Jiabao’s pledge to restore confidence in the “Made in China” brand and examining whether contaminated feed could affect meat and eggs.
counterfactuals.output:
**BEIJING (CNN) —** A series of food-safety scandals has fueled public anxiety in China and abroad, prompting Premier Wen Jiabao to pledge tougher oversight and efforts to “restore confidence in the ‘Made in China’ brand.”

The concern extends beyond products consumed directly by people. Investigators are also examining whether contaminated animal feed could carry harmful substances into pork, poultry, fish and eggs.

Food-safety specialists say the answer depends on the contaminant, its concentration and how an animal processes it. Some chemicals are quickly excreted, while others can accumulate in organs, muscle tissue or eggs. That means contaminated feed does not automatically make meat or eggs dangerous, but testing is needed to determine whether residues remain at levels that could threaten human health.

Particular attention has focused on nitrogen-rich chemicals such as melamine, which can be added illegally to make feed ingredients appear to contain more protein than they do. Melamine has been linked to kidney damage, especially when combined with related compounds that can form crystals in the urinary system.

Regulators have generally said the risk to people from eating products derived from animals exposed to low levels of contaminated feed is likely to be limited. But scientists caution that uncertainties remain, including how much of a substance animals consumed, how long they were exposed and whether multiple contaminants were present.

For Chinese consumers, the feed issue adds to broader worries about weak enforcement, fragmented supply chains and producers who cut costs by substituting unsafe ingredients. Public confidence has been shaken by repeated reports involving adulterated milk, counterfeit products, excessive pesticide residues and banned additives.

Wen said the government would strengthen inspections, punish violators and improve oversight from farms and factories to markets and ports. Restoring trust, however, may require more than new regulations. Consumer advocates say authorities must enforce existing rules consistently, disclose test results quickly and allow independent scrutiny when problems emerge.

The stakes are significant for China, one of the world’s largest food producers and exporters. Any evidence that contaminated feed has entered the human food chain could lead to recalls and trade restrictions, while also deepening unease among families already questioning the safety of everyday meals.

Experts say meat and eggs from affected farms should be held back until laboratory tests establish whether residues exceed safety limits. They also emphasize that risk should be assessed product by product rather than assuming all food from exposed animals is either safe or contaminated.

For Beijing, the challenge is both scientific and political: identifying the actual danger posed by tainted feed while convincing consumers that the government can detect problems before they reach the dinner table.
